title: How do you handle very large IN clauses, for example filtering by 10,000 ids, in JPA without hurting performance or hitting database limits?
shortTitle: Large IN clauses — chunking and alternatives?
topicTitle: Performance — Large IN, Dirty Checking, OSIV

s1_definition.profdef: Databases limit and penalize huge IN lists (Oracle caps at 1,000 literals; PostgreSQL slows as the list grows and defeats plan caching). The robust strategies are: chunk the ids into batches (e.g., 500–1,000 each) and union results, load the ids into a temporary table or an array/VALUES list and join, or push the filtering to the server side so the database never receives thousands of literals at once.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India must fetch details for 10,000 specific account numbers. Handing the clerk a single slip listing all 10,000 numbers is unwieldy — the clerk chokes, and some systems refuse slips longer than 1,000 lines. Instead you either hand over the numbers in neat bundles of 500 (chunking), or you write all 10,000 into a scratch register the clerk already has and say "match against this register" (temp table / join), which is far faster.
s1_definition.oneliner: Never dump 10K literals into one IN — chunk into batches or join against a temp table/array.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Databases limit and penalize huge IN lists (Oracle caps at 1,000 literals; PostgreSQL slows as the list grows and defeats plan caching). The robust strategies are: chunk the ids into batches (e.g., 500–1,000 each) and union results, load the ids into a temporary table or an array/VALUES list and join, or push the filtering to the server side so the database never receives thousands of literals at once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose National Bank of India must fetch details for 10,000 specific account numbers. Handing the clerk a single slip listing all 10,000 numbers is unwieldy — the clerk chokes, and some systems refuse slips longer than 1,000 lines. Instead you either hand over the numbers in neat bundles of 500 (chunking), or you write all 10,000 into a scratch register the clerk already has and say "match against this register" (temp table / join), which is far faster.

**One line to remember:** Never dump 10K literals into one IN — chunk into batches or join against a temp table/array.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach `where id in (:ids)` with 10,000 ids causes problems: Oracle throws ORA-01795 beyond 1,000 entries; PostgreSQL accepts it but generates a giant query string that defeats prepared-statement caching and bloats parse time; and binding thousands of parameters is slow.

Chunking: split the id list into partitions of, say, 1,000, run one query per chunk, and combine the results in the application. For example, with Guava `Lists.partition(ids, 1000)` or a simple loop, each query is `where id in (:chunk)` with at most 1,000 binds. This keeps each statement cacheable and within limits. The downside is multiple round-trips, but they are bounded and parallelizable.

Temporary table / join: insert the ids into a temp table (or use PostgreSQL `unnest(:idArray)` or a `VALUES` list) and join your main table against it: `SELECT a.* FROM accounts a JOIN unnest(:ids) t(id) ON a.id = t.id`. This is one query, the planner can use a hash join, and there are no literal-count limits. On PostgreSQL passing a `Long[]` and using `= ANY(:ids)` is very efficient.

Server-side filter: often the 10,000 ids are themselves the result of a query. Instead of fetching ids to the app and sending them back, keep the filter server-side as a subquery or join: `where account_id in (select id from flagged_accounts)`. This avoids moving ids over the wire entirely.

Senior nuances: for `= ANY(array)` in PostgreSQL via JPA, use a native query binding a Java array. Hibernate also has `hibernate.query.in_clause_parameter_padding` to pad IN lists to power-of-two sizes so plan caching works despite varying list lengths. Choose chunking when ids come from an external source, temp table/array for one-shot large joins, and server-side filter whenever the ids originate from the same database.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The fraud team hands National Bank of India a file of 10,000 suspicious account ids and asks for the current balance of each. A single IN with 10,000 ids would break on Oracle and crawl on PostgreSQL. This is exactly the large-IN problem.

Problem 2 — We want one efficient query rather than thousands of binds. This is exactly the array/temp-table join using `= ANY`.

Problem 3 — When the suspicious ids already come from a flagged_accounts table in the same database, we should never ship them to the app and back. This is exactly the server-side filter via subquery.

We will build an AccountLookupService offering a chunked lookup, an array-join lookup, and a server-side-filter lookup.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: 10,000 suspicious account ids from the fraud team.

Step 1 — Chunked strategy: the service slices the 10,000 ids into 10 batches of 1,000. Each batch runs `where id in (:batch)` with exactly 1,000 binds, which is within Oracle's limit and keeps the statement cacheable. The 10 result lists are concatenated.

Step 2 — Array strategy: the 10,000 ids are passed as a single Java String array to a native query `where id = ANY(:ids)`. PostgreSQL executes one query, builds a hash of the array, and hash-joins against the accounts index — a single round-trip for all 10,000.

Step 3 — Server-side strategy: if the ids live in the flagged_accounts table, the service runs `where id in (select account_id from flagged_accounts)`. No ids travel from the database to the app and back; the join happens entirely server-side.

Step 4 — All three return the matching accounts with balances. The array and server-side strategies are the fastest; chunking is the safe portable fallback.

```
INFO  Chunked lookup of 10000 ids in 10 batches
Hibernate: select ... where id in (?, ?, ... 1000 binds)   x10
INFO  Array lookup of 10000 ids in one query
Hibernate: select * from accounts a where a.id = ANY(?)
Hibernate: select a.* from accounts a where a.id in (select account_id from flagged_accounts)
```

    │
    ├─ CHUNKED
    │    split → [1000][1000]...[1000]  (10 batches)
    │    each: WHERE id IN (:batch)  (cacheable, within limits)
    │    concat results
    │
    ├─ ARRAY JOIN (= ANY)
    │    pass Long[]/String[] → WHERE id = ANY(:ids)

    ▼

```

  ┌─ Design Patterns ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Strategy: chunk / array-join / server-side filter   │

  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  │     AccountLookupService      │
  │  - CHUNK = 1000               │
  │  + lookupChunked(ids)         │ batched IN
  │  + lookupArray(ids)           │ = ANY(:ids)
  │  + lookupFlagged()            │ subquery
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                 ▼ uses
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<interface>> AccountRepo   │
  │  + findByIdChunk(List)        │
  │  + findByIdArray(String[])    │
  │  + findFlagged()              │
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Cost model ──
  10K literal IN → Oracle fails >1000, PG defeats plan cache
  chunk 1000     → 10 cacheable queries
  = ANY(array)   → 1 query, hash join
  server-side    → 0 ids over wire

  ── Call Chain (array) ──
  1. lookupArray(ids) → toArray
  2.   repo.findByIdArray(arr) → WHERE id = ANY(:ids)
  3. return matching accounts
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Dumping thousands of ids into a single IN clause is a classic mistake. Oracle rejects lists longer than a thousand entries, and PostgreSQL accepts them but generates an enormous query string that defeats prepared-statement plan caching and slows parsing, while binding thousands of parameters is itself expensive. So for a 10,000-id filter I never write one giant IN; I reach for one of three strategies depending on where the ids come from.

Chunking is the portable fallback: I split the id list into bounded batches of around a thousand, run one IN query per batch, and combine the results in the application. Each statement stays within database limits and remains cacheable, and the round-trips are bounded and can be parallelized. When I can use database-specific features, the array-join is better: I pass the ids as a single array and use a predicate like id equals ANY of the array, which PostgreSQL executes as one hash-joined query with no literal-count limit and a single round-trip. The best option, when the ids already live in the same database, is a server-side filter where I express the condition as a subquery or join so the ids never travel to the application and back at all.

In our National Bank of India system, when the fraud team hands me ten thousand suspicious account ids to look up, I use the array-join for a single efficient query. When those suspicious accounts are already recorded in a flagged-accounts table, I switch to the server-side subquery so nothing crosses the wire. Chunking is my safe default when the ids arrive from an external file and I need portability across databases.

The senior nuances I mention are Hibernate's in-clause parameter padding setting, which pads IN lists to power-of-two sizes so varying list lengths still hit the same cached plan, and the option of loading ids into a temporary table and joining when the id set is reused across many queries in one job. The guiding rule is simple: prefer server-side filtering when the ids originate in the database, use an array-join for one-shot external id sets, and fall back to bounded chunking for portability.

---

keyPoints: Chunk: split 10K IDs into 20 batches of 500
Temp table: INSERT IDs into temp table, JOIN in query
Server-side filter: subquery instead of app-side ID list
